Proof Nets for PiL (Full Version)
Matteo Acclavio, Giulia Manara

Abstract
We introduce proof nets for PiL, an extension of first-order multiplicative additive linear logic with new operators allowing a shallow encoding of processes in the π \pi -calculus as formulas. We provide correctness criterion, sequentialization procedure, and a proof translation algorithm. We show that proof nets provide a canonical representation of sequent calculus derivations modulo rule permutations.



1
Introduction

The system
\mathsf{PiL}
is an extension of (a particular case of)

first-order multiplicative additive linear logic
(
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
) with two new operators:
a non-commutative non-associative self-dual connective (
\blacktriangleleft
), and a nominal quantifier
1
1

1

In the sense of Pitt’s and Gabbay’s nominal logic
[
26
,
9
]
, which is a logic for reasoning about names and binding, where the nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
allows to express freshness conditions on variables.

(
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
) together with its dual (
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
).
It has been introduced in
[
4
]
to prove the completeness of choreographic programming
[
22
]
with respect to (race-free) deadlock-free processes of the
\pi
-calculus
[
21
]
.
Thanks to the
\blacktriangleleft
modeling sequential composition, and the nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
modelling name binding,
\mathsf{PiL}
provides a logical framework allowing for a shallow encoding of processes as formulas, and for a proof-theoretic account of execution of processes as proof-search.
In particular, the completeness result relies on the correspondence between cut-free derivations in
\mathsf{PiL}
and choreographies.
This correspondence relies on the fact that proof equivalence in
\mathsf{PiL}
induced by independent rule permutations captures the semantics of execution trees of processes modulo the interleaving of independent actions, and the natural equivalence between choreographies modulo the mechanism of out-of-order execution.
For this reason, the study of proof equivalence in
\mathsf{PiL}
is a way to study the semantics of processes in the
\pi
-calculus, and of choreographies.
In this paper, we provide formalisms for proofs in
\mathsf{PiL}
providing canonical representation of sequent calculus derivations modulo different classes of independent rule permutations to provide the basis for developing new tools to study the semantics of process calculi.

We build on the rich literature on
proof nets
for linear logic (see, e.g.,
[
10
,
6
,
11
,
28
,
5
,
18
,
16
,
14
,
13
]
), a graph-based formalism for proofs that has been widely studied as a solution to the problem of proof identity in proof theory.
Proof nets achieve canonicity by replacing sequent rules with graphical constructors that minimize dependencies between inference steps, thereby collapsing entire classes of sequent derivations into a single syntactic object.
However, the syntax of proof nets is strictly more expressive than that of the sequent calculus. It admits the construction of terms, called
proof structures
, that do not correspond to valid derivations.
For this reason, every proof net formalism must be equipped with a (polynomial-time)
correctness criterion
that identifies the proof structures representing valid proofs, together with a polynomial-time
sequentialization procedure
translating proof nets back into sequent derivations.

Proof nets for the multiplicative fragment of linear logic can be seen as a decoration of the parse tree of the conclusion of a proof with
axiom links
connecting leaves which are dual atoms.

(1)

Correctness can be characterized either by checking acyclicity and connectivity conditions on associated graphs
[
6
,
27
]
, or by verifying that the structure contracts to a single vertex under a system of rewriting rules
[
7
]
.

Additives complicate this picture because the inference rule for the additive conjunction
\with
requires context duplication.
This requires proof nets to track the ‘additive branching’ structure of the proof which is of a different nature with respect to the ‘multiplicative branching’ structure induced by the
\mathop{\otimes}
rule.

(2)

For this reason, correctness criteria for proof nets for
\mathsf{MALL}
require a richer structure.
In Girard’s
monomial nets

[
12
]
, this is achieved by annotating axiom links with Boolean variables.
In Hughes and Heijltjes’
conflict nets

[
17
,
14
]
, axiom links are organized into trees, where they are related either by a ‘multiplicative’ concordance relation or by an ‘additive’ conflict relation.

(3)

Quantifiers introduce additional complexity in the definition of proof nets, as they require tracking the witnesses of quantification and the potential dependencies between them.
For example, the following two derivations may be considered non-equivalent, since the witnesses of the existential quantifiers are different.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

The information required to distinguish the two derivations in
Equation

4
is captured by associating each link with
a substitution, called a
dualizer
, mapping the variables occurring in the link to the corresponding existential witnesses.
The name
dualizer
reflects the fact that a link may connect atoms that are not yet dual, and that it is the dualizer that
enforces duality by unifying them.
The derivations in
Equation

4
yield the same links but different dualizers:
In the one on the left (resp. right), the witnesses of the existential quantifiers is the variable
z
(resp.
w
), and the duality between
P(x)
and
{P(y)}^{\bot}
is enforced by the dualizer
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}=[z/x,z/y]
(resp.
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}}=[w/x,w/y]
).

(5)

1.1
Challenges

We adopt
conflict nets
as the main underlying framework for proof nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
, as they provide a good trade-off between canonicity, computational complexity of correctness criterion, sequentialization procedure, and proof translation algorithm
2
2

2

We remind the reader that cut-elimination for conflict nets is not efficient.
However, in this paper we are interested in proof nets as canonical representatives of
cut-free
proofs, since in
[
4
]
they are used to represent both computation trees of processes and choreographies.
Therefore, we are not interested in study the semantics of cut-elimination in this paper, which present additional challenges we shall address in future work.

.
Note that the only proof nets for
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
available in the literature are the ones based on Girard’s proof nets, which present some issues in terms of canonicity and computational efficiency of the proof translation
[
16
,
14
]
.
At the same time, works such as
[
19
]
and
[
13
]
provide techniques for handling quantifiers in the multiplicative fragment and additive fragment of linear logic based on contractability correctness criteria similar to the ones for conflict nets.
However, so far these techniques have never been studied in presence of both multiplicative and additive connectives.

Another challenge in defining proof nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
is the presence of the non-commutative and non-associative connective
\blacktriangleleft
, it has strong connections with the connective
\triangleleft
of Retoré’s
pomset logic

[
27
,
29
]
, for which no contractability correctness criterion is known, and Guglielmi’s
\mathsf{BV}
logic, for which no correctness criterion for proof nets is known.
However, the connective
\blacktriangleleft
is weaker than the
\triangleleft
since the latter prevents the existence of a cut-free sequent calculus
[
31
,
24
,
23
]
. At the same time,
\blacktriangleleft
is fundamentally different from the non-commutative connectives studied in works such as
[
32
,
1
]
, which are associative and not self-dual.

Finally, our nominal quantifiers require a fine bookkeeping of the freshness conditions on variables to guarantees that nominal quantified variables can be shared by at most a unique pair of dual nominal quantifiers.
This is a novel feature (even with respect to other logics with nominal quantifiers), requires novel techniques.

1.2
Contributions

We define
conflict nets
for
\mathsf{PiL}
, and we provide a (polynomial-time) correctness criterion, a proof translation algorithm, and a sequentialization procedure.
Then, we provide a rewriting to reduce conflict nets to canonical form, called
slice nets
while preserving the correctness of the structure.
For both proof nets, we prove canonicity results, showing that they provide a canonical representation of sequent calculus derivations modulo distinct classes of independent rule permutations.

1.3
Structure of the paper

In
Section

2
we recall the definition and the main properties of the sequent system
\mathsf{PiL}
, we recall the notation for substitutions, and the definition of links and their dualizers, which will be used in the definition of proof nets.
In
Section

3
we define conflict nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
, and we provide a correctness criterion, a proof translation algorithm, and a sequentialization procedure.
In
Section

4
we define slice nets and we show how they can be obtained from conflict nets by a rewriting procedure called
flattening
.
In
Section

5
we show that conflict nets and slice nets provide a canonical representation of sequent calculus derivations modulo distinct classes of independent rule permutations.
We conclude in
Section

6
with a discussion of the results, and of future work.

Because of space constraints, some proofs are only sketched in the main text, and are fully detailed in
Appendix

0.A
.

2
Background

The sequent system
\mathsf{PiL}
is an extension (of a special case) of
first-order multiplicative additive linear logic
(
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
) obtained by including new operators allowing for a faithful embedding of processes of the
\pi
-calculus as formulas
[
4
]
: the connective
\blacktriangleleft
allows to represent the sequential composition of processes, while the nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
allows to represent name restriction and name passing.
In this section we recall the definition of
\mathsf{PiL}
and some of its properties, which will be useful for the definition of proof nets in the next sections.

We consider
formulas
generated from a countable set of variables
\mathcal{V}
and the dual binary predicate symbols

send
(
\langle-\oc-\rangle
) and

receive
(
(-\wn-)
),
the
unit
(
\circ
),
the binary connectives

par
(
\invamp
),

tensor
(
\mathop{\otimes}
),

prec
(
\blacktriangleleft
),

oplus
(
\mathop{\oplus}
), and

with
(
\with
),
the standard

universal
(
\forall
) and

existential
(
\exists
) quantifiers,
and the nominal quantifiers

new
(
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
) and

ya
(
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
)
using the following grammar

A,B\coloneqq a\mid A\odot B\mid\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A\quad\text{with }\begin{cases}a\in\{\circ,\langle x\oc y\rangle,(x\wn y)\mid x,y\in\mathcal{V}\}\text{ {\boldmath atomic}}\\
\odot\in\{\invamp,\mathop{\otimes},\blacktriangleleft,\mathop{\oplus},\with\}\\
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}\in\{\forall,\exists,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\},\quad x\in\mathcal{V}\end{cases}

(6)

modulo the
\alpha
-equivalence
generated by the following equations:

\begin{array}[]{r@{\;\alphaeq\;}l@{\quad}l}a\;\equiv_{\alpha}&a&\mbox{if $a\in\{\circ,\langle x\oc y\rangle,(x\wn y)\mid x,y\in\mathcal{V}\}$}\\
A_{1}\circleddot A_{2}\;\equiv_{\alpha}&B_{1}\circleddot B_{2}&\mbox{if $A_{i}\equiv_{\alpha}B_{i}$ and $\circleddot\in\{\invamp,\blacktriangleleft,\mathop{\otimes},\mathop{\oplus},\with\}$}\\
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A\;\equiv_{\alpha}&\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{y}.A[y/x]&\mbox{if $y$ fresh for $A$ and $\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}},\forall,\exists\}$}\end{array}

(7)

We say that a quantification
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A
with
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}\in\{\forall,\exists,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}

binds
the occurrences of the variable
x
in
A
, and define the set of
free variables
of a formula
A
as the set
\mathsf{free}(A)
of variables occurring in
A
which are not bound by any quantifier.
To simplify our presentation, in this paper we identify formulas and their
formula-trees
, that is, we assume each atom, connective, and quantifier in a formula to be uniquely identified by its corresponding node in the formula-tree of the formula.

A
sequent

\Gamma
is a set of occurrences of formulas, or, equivalently, a forest of formula trees.
Its set of
free variables

\mathsf{free}(\Gamma)
are the union of the free variables of the formulas occurring in
\Gamma
.

Definition 1

A
nominal variable
is an element of the form
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\nabla}}
with
x\in\mathcal{V}
and

\nabla\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}
.
If
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
is a set of nominal variables, we say that
x

occurs
in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
if
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
or

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
is an element of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
.
A
(nominal) store

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
is a set of nominal variables such that each variable occurs at most once in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
.
We denote by
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{1},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{2}
the union of two stores
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{1}
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{2}
sharing no variable.

A
judgement
(for a sequent
\Gamma
) is an expression of the form
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
with
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
a store such that variables occurring in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
are free in
\Gamma
.
We may write
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{1}^{\nabla_{1}}},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{n}^{\nabla_{n}}}}}\vdash\Gamma
for the judgement
\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{1}^{\nabla_{1}}},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{n}^{\nabla_{n}}}\}\vdash\Gamma
and
simply
\vdash\Gamma
for the judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\varnothing}\vdash\Gamma
.

Notation 2.1

From now on, we always assume judgements and sequents to be
clean
, meaning that each variable
x
may occur bound by at most one quantifier, and if it occurs bound or in the store, then cannot occur free in the sequent.
Note however, that we may provide examples with non-clean judgements to improve readability and to highlight the connection between variables bound by dual quantifiers.

The system
\mathsf{PiL}
is defined by all rules in
Figure

1
.
The left-hand side of the figure shows the standard rules for
first-order multiplicative additive linear logic
(
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
) decorated with stores.
On the right-hand side we recall the rules for the (self-dual) unit
\circ
, and for the
\blacktriangleleft
operator, as well as the rules for nominal quantifiers.
The rule for the
\blacktriangleleft
is
multiplicative
(in this sense of
[
6
,
12
,
2
]
) and can introduce any number of
\blacktriangleleft
-formulas at once; the case
n=0
corresponds to the
\mathsf{mix}
rule.
The rules
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ}
and
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ}
simply remove the nominal quantifier while respecting the freshness condition (
\dagger
), as the standard rule
\forall
for the universal quantifier.
Similarly, the rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
) removes quantification while respecting the same freshness condition of universal quantification (
\dagger
), and additionally loads the fresh variable
x
, bound by the nominal quantifier, as a nominal variable
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
) in the store.
The rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}
) behaves similarly to the rule
\exists
for the existential quantifier, but uses as a witness of the quantification a nominal variable
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}y^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}y^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
) in the store, consuming it.
The combination of the rules
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
and
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
and
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}
),
together with the linear control of resources of the conjunction rules,
guarantees that each nominal variable can be used as witness for at most one nominal quantification.

:
Sequent calculus rules of
\mathsf{PiL}
, where

.

Notation 2.2

We write
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\Gamma
to denote the existence of a derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
with conclusion the judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\varnothing}\vdash\Gamma
.
We denote by

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma

a derivation with conclusion
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
.

Remark 1

In the definition of
\mathsf{PiL}
, we did not discuss the definition of negation, which is defined by extending the one of
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
by the De Morgan laws
{\circ}^{\bot}=\circ
,
{(A\blacktriangleleft B)}^{\bot}={A}^{\bot}\blacktriangleleft{B}^{\bot}
, and
{(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A)}^{\bot}=\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.({A}^{\bot})
.
However, for the purpose of this paper, it suffices to only keep in mind that
\langle-\oc-\rangle
and
(-\wn-)
, as well as that two nominal quantifiers, are dual to each other.

Similarly, we do not discuss the cut rule because it has no computational interpretation in the proof-search semantics of
\mathsf{PiL}
from
[
4
]
.
However, cut-elimination for
\mathsf{PiL}
holds, and its proof requires a non-trivial treatment of the nominal quantifiers and the store. Details are provided in
[
3
]
.

Notation 2.3

For brevity, we may denote by
\nabla
any nominal quantifier, and when we write
{\nabla}^{\bot}
we assume that
{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}^{\bot}=\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
and
{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}^{\bot}=\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
.

2.1
Links, Substitutions, and Dualizers

We conclude this section by recalling and extending the definitions of
link
and
dualizer
from the literature.

Definition 2

A
link

{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
on a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
is either:

•

a
sub-sequent
of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
, that is, a sequent
\Gamma^{\prime}
which is a sub-forest of
\Gamma
;

•

or a
nominal link
, that is, either

–

a two-elements set
\{x,y\}\subset\mathcal{V}
of variables occurring in
\Gamma
such that
x
is bound by
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
and
y
is bound by a
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
; or

–

a two-elements set
\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}},y\}
(resp.
\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}},y\}
) consisting of a nominal variable
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
) occurring in the store and a variable
y
occurring in
\Gamma
bound by the nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
);

A link is
axiomatic
if it is of the form
\{\circ\}
or
\{\langle x\oc y\rangle,(z\wn t)\}
,
or if it is a nominal link of the form
\{x,y\}\subset\mathcal{V}
containing no nominal variable.

A
linking
(resp.
axiomatic linking
) on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
is a set of links
(resp. axiomatic links) on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
.

Notation 2.4

We represent a link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
by drawing a horizontal line labeled by
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
connected via vertical segments
to each (root of a) subformula and to each variable in the link.
For example,

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}z}=\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}z^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}},v\}
,
{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}{c}}}=\{x,y\}
,
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{A,C,D\mathop{\oplus}E\}
, and
{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}=\{B,(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.C)\invamp(D\oplus E),\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{y}.F\}
are valid links for the judgement below, which has been decorated with the links to show how they are represented.

(8)

Note that
\{D,D\oplus E\}
is not a link for the judgement above because the formula
D
is repeated twice, therefore is not a sub-forest of the sequent in the judgement.

A
substitution

\sigma=[x_{1}/y_{1},\ldots,x_{n}/y_{n}]
is a map with domain
\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\}\subset\mathcal{V}
and image
\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\subset\mathcal{V}
.
3
3

3

Note that we assume substitutions to map variables to variables because we have no function symbols in
\mathsf{PiL}
, that is, terms are variables only.

If
X
is a formula (resp. variable or judgement), we write
\sigma(X)
or
X\sigma
for the formula (resp. variable or judgement) obtained from
X
by simultaneously substituting each occurrence of the variable
y_{i}
with an occurrence of the variable
x_{i}
for all
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
.

Notation 2.5

We adopt the following notation for substitutions:

•

\delta_{\varnothing}
for the
empty substitution
;

•

\sigma\tau
for the
composition
of
\sigma
and
\tau
(in which
\sigma
is applied
after

\tau
);

•

\sigma\setminus\{x\}
for the substitution obtained restricting
\sigma
by removing the variable
x
from its domain, and
\sigma x
from its image;

•

\sigma\geq\rho
if
\sigma
for
more general
than
\tau
, that is, if
\sigma=\tau\rho
for some
\tau
;

•

\mathsf{coh}(\sigma,\tau)
if

\sigma
and
\tau
are
coherent
on their domains, that is, if
x\in\mathsf{dom}(\sigma)\cap\mathsf{dom}(\tau)
then
\sigma(x)=\tau(x)
;

•

\sigma\vee\tau
for the most general map
\rho
such that
\sigma\leq\rho
and
\tau\leq\rho
;

Definition 3

A
dualizer

\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}
for a link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
on a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
is a substitution whose domain consists of

•

one of the two variables in
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
is a nominal link; or

•

variables occurring in
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
bound by an existential quantifier (
\exists
) or nominal quantifier (
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
or
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
) in
\Gamma
otherwise.

A
witness map

\delta^{\Lambda}
for a linking
\Lambda
is a map associating a (possibly empty) dualizer
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}
to each link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
in
\Lambda
.
If
\Lambda
is an axiomatic linking, then we say that a witness map
\delta^{\Lambda}
for
\Lambda
is
valid
if the following conditions hold for each
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}\in\Lambda
:

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{\langle x\oc y\rangle,(z\wn t)\}
, then
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}(x)=\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}(z)
and
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}(y)=\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}(t)
;

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{x,y\}
is an axiomatic nominal link, then
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}(x)=\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}(y)
;

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{\circ\}
, then
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}=\delta_{\varnothing}
.

3
Conflict Nets

Conflict nets for
\mathsf{MALL}

[
14
]
are trees alternating
concord
(
\frown
) and
conflict
(
\#
) nodes and axiomatic links as leaves, and satisfying a contractability criterion with respect to a rewriting procedure called
coalescence
.
Intuitively, leaves of these trees represent derivable sequents, and each coalescence step checks that an inference rule of the system can correctly apply to construct a new derivable sequent from the ones involved in the step. That is, coalescence checks that the structure of the proof net correctly reflects to the top-down construction of a derivation in the sequent calculus.
In this section, we extend the definition of conflict nets to the first-order setting of
\mathsf{PiL}
.

We recall the definition of
concord-conflict tree
from
[
14
]
.

Definition 4

A
concord-conflict tree
(or
coco-tree
for short) for a linking
\Lambda
on a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
is a tree
\tau(\Lambda)
with
\Lambda
as its set of leaves,
and internal nodes labeled by
\frown
(
concord
nodes) or by
\#
(
conflict
nodes).
We denote by
\left\lfloor\tau(\Lambda)\right\rfloor
the
canonization
of a coco-tree
\Lambda
, that is, the coco-tree obtained by merging adjacent
\frown
-nodes (resp.
\#
-nodes), and by removing nodes with a single child by attaching its child to its parent.
A coco-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
is
axiomatic
if
\Lambda
is so; it is
canonical
if
\tau(\Lambda)=\left\lfloor\tau(\Lambda)\right\rfloor
.

We enrich the definition of conflict nets and coalescence from
[
14
]
with the information about witnesses, which is required to properly deal with quantifiers in the first-order setting similarly to
[
18
,
13
,
15
]
.

Definition 5

A
pre-structure
is a pair
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle
on
\Gamma
made of a coco-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
and a witness map
\delta^{\Lambda}
for the linking
\Lambda
of
\tau(\Lambda)
.
It is
trivial
if
\tau(\Lambda)
consists of a single leaf
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
and
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}=\delta_{\varnothing}
.
A
proof structure
for a sequent
\Gamma
is a pre-structure
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta\rangle
where
\tau(\Lambda)
is axiomatic and canonical, and
\delta^{\Lambda}
is valid.

A
proof net

\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle
for a sequent
\Gamma

is a proof structure for
\Gamma
which is also
coalescent
, that is, it admits a sequence of

coalescence steps
from
Figure

2
transforming
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta\rangle
into a trivial pre-structure.
See
Figure

2
for an example.

Figure 2
:
Coalescence steps for
\mathsf{PiL}
.

We can define the proof translation by translating top-down the rules of a given derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
as shown in
Figure

3
, allowing us to prove that our conflict nets are complete with respect to
\mathsf{PiL}
.

Lemma 1

Let
\Gamma
be a sequent.
If
\mathcal{D}
is a derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
with conclusion
\Gamma
,
then there is a conflict net for
\Gamma
.

Proof

We define
\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}\!=\langle\tau(\mathcal{D}),\delta^{\mathcal{D}}\rangle
by translating top-down the rules of
\mathcal{D}
using the construction in
Figure

3
, where
we denote by
\tau_{1}\frown\tau_{2}
(resp.
\tau_{1}\#\tau_{2}
) the coco-tree with root a
\frown
-node (resp.
\#
-node) having as children the roots of
\tau_{1}
and
\tau_{2}
.
Note that the translation uses the (not necessarily sound) rule
\mathsf{leaf}
which generalizes
\mathsf{ax}
up-to the existence of a proper unifier.
This is due to the necessity of updating the witness map and the leaves of the coco-tree if we want to give an inductive translation of derivations in
\mathsf{PiL}
which is compositional with respect to the structure of the derivation.

To prove that
\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}\!
is coalescent, it suffices to consider the sequence of coalescence steps corresponding to the
\mathsf{PiL}
rules used in the proof, in the same order in which the rules of
\mathcal{D}
have been translated: each side condition for the coalescence steps in
Figure

2
is satisfied by construction.
Moreover, in the translation of the rules
\exists
,
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
, and
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
, the witness map is updated so that, once the corresponding quantifier is coalesced, the associated dualizers are ‘emptied’.

:

Translation of a derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
into a conflict net,
with

{\mathsf{r}^{1}}\in\{\invamp,\oplus,\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}^{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}\}
,
and

{\mathsf{r}^{2}}\in\{\mathop{\otimes},\blacktriangleleft\}
,
and
where we denote by

\mathcal{D}_{x}
(resp.
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{x}
) the derivation (resp. link) obtained from
\mathcal{D}_{y}
(resp.
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{y}
) by replacing all occurrences of the variable
y
involved in the rule
{\mathsf{r}}\in\{\exists,\nabla_{\mathsf{pop}}\}
with
x
and where
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{x}}^{\mathcal{D}}=[y/x]\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{y}}^{\mathcal{D}_{y}}
if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{x}\neq{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{y}
and
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{y}}^{\mathcal{D}_{y}}
otherwise.

To prove the adequacy of conflict nets with respect to
\mathsf{PiL}
, it now suffices to provide a sequentialization procedure associating to a given conflict net for
\Gamma
a derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
with conclusion
\Gamma
.

Theorem 3.1

There is a conflict net
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta\rangle
for
\Gamma

iff
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\Gamma
.

Proof

The right-to-left implication is consequence of
Lemma

1
.

To prove the other implication, we provide a sequentialization procedure for conflict nets to construct a derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
from a given conflict net for
\Gamma
by induction on the length
n
of a coalescence path for the conflict net, which exists by definition of coalescent coco-tree with witnesses.
We define
deductive coco-trees
pre-structures where leaves which are sequents (i.e., not nominal links) are labeled by derivations with conclusion of a judgement for the given sequent.

If
n=0
, then the conflict net is trivial.
The only possible cases are if either
\Gamma=\circ
or
\Gamma=\langle x\oc y\rangle,(x\wn y)
for some
x,y\in\mathcal{V}
since
\delta_{\Gamma}
must be valid and empty.
In both cases, we can easily construct a derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
with conclusion
\Gamma
by applying the rules
\circ
or
\mathsf{leaf}
respectively.

If
n>0
, then we reason by cases on the last coalescence step in the coalescence path as shown in
Figure

4
, reminding the reader that the coalescence steps defined ‘top-down’ operating on leaves.
In particular, each coalescence step corresponds to a rule of
\mathsf{PiL}
, the side conditions for the coalescence steps ensure that the corresponding rule of
\mathsf{PiL}
can be applied, and the new leaf produced by the coalescence step is labeled by a derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
obtained by applying the corresponding rule to the derivations labeling the leaves which are coalesced.

Figure 4
:

Effect of coalescence steps in
Figure

2
on coco-trees with leaves labeled by derivations.
The steps
\bullet
and
\#
change no link labels.

The
size
of a conflict net
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle
for a sequent
\Gamma
is the number
|\tau(\Lambda)|
of nodes in the coco-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
plus the size of the sequent
\Gamma
.

Proposition 1

It is possible to check if a coco-tree with witnesses is coalescent in polynomial time with respect to its size.

Proof

The result follows from the same argument (and algorithms) used in
[
14
]
in the proof of the similar result for
\mathsf{MALL}
, where the complexity is
\mathcal{O}(n^{4})
.

The new multiplicative coalescence steps (the ones involving the
\blacktriangleleft
) are as complex as the
\mathop{\otimes}
. Note that the additional side condition on the
\mathop{\otimes}
and
\blacktriangleleft
steps can be checked in linear time with respect to the size of the formula (tree).
The additional manipulations of the dualizers are all linear in the size of the dualizer (see
[
20
]
), thus linear in the size of the formula.
Thus, complexity has an upper bound of
\mathcal{O}(n^{5})
.

4
Slice nets

In this section, we define
slice net
as special conflict net whose underlying coco-tree is ‘flat’, i.e., it has at most a single
\#
-node at its root.
While correctness of slice nets follows from the result on conflict nets, to prove the converse we introduce a procedure allowing us to transform any conflict net into a slice net.

Definition 6

A
slice net
for a sequent
\Gamma
is a conflict net
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle
(for
\Gamma
) such that the underlying coco-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
has at most a single
\#
-node at its root.

The flattening procedure, seen on coco-trees, consists of moving
\frown
-nodes above
\#
-nodes in a coco-tree.
This is done by moving all children of a
\frown
-node except one of its
\#
-child above this latter, by replacing each child of the selected
\#
-node with a
\frown
-node having as children the selected
\#
-child and all the children of
\frown
-node we want to move up.
Formally, this is done by applying the following rewriting rule on coco-trees.

Definition 7

A
flattening step
on coco-trees is defined by the following rewriting rule on graphs

(10)

where
\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{n},\tau^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,\tau^{\prime}_{m}
are coco-trees, and where the dotted edge represent, when it exists, the edge connecting root of the subtree on which we apply the flattening step to its parent.
Flattening extends to conflict nets by applying the flattening step on the underlying coco-tree, and preserving the dualizer for each of the copied link.

We call
flattening
the rewriting relation defined by the flattening steps.

We then prove that the normal forms of flattening are unique, and that flattening preserves coalescence.

:
Convergence of the non-trivial critical pair for flattening.

Lemma 2

Flattening is strongly normalizing and has a unique normal form.

Proof

Flattening admits a unique form of non-trivial critical pairs, which is confluent (see
Figure

5
).

To prove termination, we define a measure
\mu
on coco-trees defined as follows:
if the root of
\tau
is a leaf, then
\mu(\tau)=2
;
if
\tau=\#(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})
, then
\mu(\tau)=\mu(\tau_{1})+\mu(\tau_{2})+1
;
and if
\tau=\frown(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})
, then
\mu(\tau)=\mu(\tau_{1})\cdot\mu(\tau_{2})
.
Each flattening step strictly decreases the measure of the coco-tree:
let
\tau
be the subcoco-tree rooted at the
\#
on the left-hand side of
Equation

10
,
and let
\tau^{\prime}
be the subcoco-tree on the right-hand side.
By construction
m>0
, thus

\mu(\tau)=(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu(\tau_{i})+1)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\tau^{\prime}_{i})>\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu(\tau_{i})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\tau^{\prime}_{i})+1\geq\mu(\tau^{\prime})
.
The last inequality follows from the fact that the operation of canonization (
\left\lfloor\cdot\right\rfloor
) further reduces the measure.

Therefore, flattening is terminating, and by Newman’s Lemma, it is confluent, yielding the uniqueness of normal forms.

Theorem 4.1

Let
\mathcal{P}
be a conflict net.
If
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
be is the normal form of
\mathcal{P}
with respect to flattening, then
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
is a slice net.

Proof

Flattening preserves the fact that the coco-tree is axiomatic, and it is defined to preserve canonicity.
Moreover, the validity of the witness map is preserved by the fact that flattening may ‘duplicate’ links and their dualizer, but it does not change the dualizer of any link.
To conclude, we have to show that flattening preserves coalescence.

Thanks to
Lemma

2
, we can assume that the
\#
-node involved in the flattening step is the root of
\tau(\Lambda)
, because we can always assume the coalescence path first reduces the coco-tree rooted in the
\#
-node involved in the flattening step, and that no coalescence steps can be applied to
\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{n},\tau^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,\tau^{\prime}_{m}
, in particular, that they are coco-trees made of a single link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{1},\ldots,{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{n},{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{1},\ldots,{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{m}
respectively.

If
n=2
, then we know we can apply a
\with
-step to
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{1}
and
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{2}
, obtaining a link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
, and then, after a
\bullet
-step, we know we can apply some coalescence steps from the ones in the top part of
Figure

2
on
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
and
{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{1},\ldots,{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{n}
until the coco-tree coalesces on a single link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a^{\prime}}}}
.

Therefore, we know that the same sequence of coalescence steps can be applied to
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{1},{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{1},\ldots,{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{m}
and to
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{2},{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{1},\ldots,{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}_{m}

reaching links
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a^{\prime}_{1}}}}
and
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a^{\prime}_{2}}}}
respectively, since both
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{1}
and
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}_{2}
are sub-sequents of
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
.

We can now conclude the proof of the main result of this section, which states that slice nets are sound and complete for
\mathsf{PiL}
.

Theorem 4.2

Let
\Gamma
be a sequent.
Then
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\Gamma
iff there is a slice net for
\Gamma
.

Proof

It follows from the result on conflict nets
Theorem

3.1
and the fact that flattening preserves coalescence (
Theorem

4.1
).

Figure 6
:

Rule permutations
in
\mathsf{PiL}

with

\mathsf{\beta},\mathsf{\beta}_{1},\mathsf{\beta}_{2}\in\{\mathop{\otimes},\blacktriangleleft\}

and with

\mathsf{\alpha},\mathsf{\alpha}_{1},\mathsf{\alpha}_{2}\in\{\invamp,\mathop{\oplus},\exists,\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}^{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}^{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}\}
.

In this section we discuss the proof equivalence enforced by conflict nets and slice nets, called
local
and
strong
canonicity, respectively.

For this, we define two equivalence relations over derivations, and a notion of isomorphism for conflict nets (and thus for slice nets) which we use to state the canonicity results.

Definition 8

We define the two following equivalence relations over derivations in
\mathsf{PiL}
using the rule permutations in
Figure

6
:

•

local equivalence
(denoted
\mathcal{D}_{1}\approx\mathcal{D}_{2}
) if it is possible to transform
\mathcal{D}_{1}
into
\mathcal{D}_{2}
using a sequence of local rule permutations;

•

strong equivalence
(denoted
\mathcal{D}_{1}\simeq\mathcal{D}_{2}
) if it is possible to transform
\mathcal{D}_{1}
into
\mathcal{D}_{2}
using a sequence of both local and non-local rule permutations.

Definition 9

Two conflict nets
\langle\Lambda_{1},\delta_{1}\rangle
and
\langle\Lambda_{2},\delta_{2}\rangle

are
isomorphic
(denoted
\langle\Lambda_{1},\delta_{1}\rangle=\langle\Lambda_{2},\delta_{2}\rangle
)
if there is a label-preserving isomorphism between
\Lambda_{1}
and
\Lambda_{2}
and such that
\delta_{1}=\delta_{2}
.

Lemma 3

Let
\mathcal{P}=\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle
be a conflict net for
\Gamma
and
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}}
be a derivation obtained by sequentializing it.
If
\mathcal{P}\xrightarrow{}^{*}\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
,
then
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
can be sequentialized into a derivation
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}^{\prime}}
such that
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}^{\prime}}\approx\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}}
.

Proof

It is sufficient to show that all critical pairs of coalescence steps converge and that the resulting derivations are equivalent modulo the local rule permutations shown in
Figure

6
.
The most convoluted case is the one for the pair
\#/\#
, which can be treated in the exact same way as in
[
13
]
after remarking that
the additional information provided by the witness map does not interfere with the proof because the join operator on dualizers is associative and commutative.
The cases which are not present in
[
14
]
are discussed in
Appendix

0.A
.

Lemma 4

Let
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
be two conflict nets for
\Gamma
and let
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}}
and
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}^{\prime}}
be two derivations obtained by sequentializing them.
If
\mathcal{P}\Rightarrow\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
, then
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}^{\prime}}\simeq\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}}
.

Proof

For the same reasons of the ones used in the proof of
Theorem

4.1
, we only discuss the case in which the flattening step is applied to the root of the coco-tree, that the
\#
-node affected by the step has only two children, and that no coalescence step can be applied in the subtree affected by flattening.

To simplify the reasoning, use the following
small-step
reduction

Theorem 5.1

Let
\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
be two derivations in
\mathsf{PiL}
.
Then,

1.

\mathcal{D}\approx\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
iff
\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}\!=\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}\!
.

2.

\mathcal{D}\simeq\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
iff
\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}=\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}
.

where we denote by
\left\{\!\!\left\{\cdot\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}
the function mapping a derivation to the slice net obtained by flattening the conflict net associated to it via
\left\{\!\!\left\{\cdot\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}\!
defined in
Figure

3
.

Proof

To prove the left-to-right implication of both points, it suffices to show that if
\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
are two derivations with the bottom-most rules in a configuration as in
Figure

6
, then
\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}\!=\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}\!
and
\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}=\left\{\!\!\left\{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\right\}\!\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}
, respectively.
For the rules in
\mathsf{MALL}
, the proof is the one in
[
14
]
and
[
16
]
, respectively, and the additional cases for the rules of
\mathsf{PiL}
are straightforward.

The right-to-left implication of
Item

1
follows from
Lemma

3
since each non-trivial critical pair of coalescence steps corresponds to a local rule permutation in
Figure

6
.
The right-to-left implication of

is more involved.
It relies on

(flattening preserves coalescence), and

6
Conclusion and Perspectives

In this paper we defined
conflict nets
and
slice nets
for
\mathsf{PiL}
, proved their soundness and completeness, provided sequentialization procedures and proof translations, and studied the proof equivalences they capture.

The results presented here, in conjunction with the ones in
[
4
]
, open to the possibility of using proof nets as a basis for the study of the semantics of concurrent systems.
For example, a direct correspondence between choreographies and proof nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
can be easily obtained by combining the proof translation from this paper and the results in
[
4
]
.

Moreover, the canonicity results we proved suggest that proof nets can provide a canonical representatives of execution trees for concurrent programs, since they allow to identify execution trees while ignoring irrelevant differences (such as permutations of independent actions), while still distinguishing execution trees that differ due to externally observable phenomena (such as race conditions or side effects).
The distinction between local and strong canonicity also suggests that different notions of proof equivalence may be relevant for the definition of different notions of equivalences for concurrent systems, depending on the specific requirements of the application at hand.
For instance, local canonicity may be more suitable for applications where the order of branching during an exectution is relevant, while strong canonicity may be more suitable for applications where the order of branching is irrelevant, such as in the case of bisimulation equivalences for concurrent systems.

In future work, we may study cut-elimination for our proof nets, where the mechanics of nominal quantifiers is far for being trivial, and, already in the sequent calculus, it requires additional rules
[
3
]
.
We expect that proof nets for first-order multiplicative additive linear logic can be obtained by a straightforward extension of our definitions, allowing for general terms and predicate symbols (and removing unit, the
\blacktriangleleft
, and nominal quantifiers, as well as the corresponding coalescence steps).
4
4

4

In this setting, an axiomatic linking
\Lambda
on
\Gamma
consists of links of the form
\{P(t_{1},\dots,t_{n}),{P}^{\bot}(s_{1},\dots,s_{n})\}
, and the dualizer for each such link is a substitution (with the same constarins on their domain as in
Definition

3
) unifying
P(t_{1},\dots,t_{n})
and
P(s_{1},\dots,s_{n})
.

Such proof nets could be used to extend the result on interpolation for linear logic
[
30
,
8
]
, relying on proof nets with contractability correctness criteria similar to the one we used for conflict nets.

Concerning the nominal quantifiers, proof nets underlay again their ‘linear’ nature in handling fresh names, which suggest them as a possible basis for the study of ‘multiplicative’ quantifiers (see, e.g.,
[
25
]
)
Finally, an important open question is the characterization of the proof equivalence induced by abstracting from the witnesses of nominal quantifiers, thus defining a stronger notion of proof equivalence reflecting the agnostic nature of nominal quantifiers with respect to the choice of fresh names, as well as of all quantifiers as in
[
18
,
13
]

(see
Appendix

0.B
for a preliminary discussion on this topic).

\delta_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{ab}}}=\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}
,

\delta_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{a^{\prime}}}}=\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}\setminus\{y\}

\delta_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{a^{\prime}b}}}=\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}\setminus\{y\}

Case
{\mathsf{r}}/\#
with
{\mathsf{r}}\in\{\exists,\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ}\}
:

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l},b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c)&\to&\#(\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l}),\#(b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c))\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l},b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c^{\prime})&\to&\#(\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l}),\#(b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c^{\prime}))\end{array}

Where either

–

{\mathsf{r}}\in\{\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}\}
, thus

c=\Gamma,A
,
c^{\prime}=\Gamma,\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A
, and
\delta_{c^{\prime}}=\delta_{c}
; or

–

{\mathsf{r}}\in\{\exists,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\}
, thus

c=\Gamma,A
,
c^{\prime}=\Gamma,\exists{x}.A
and
\delta_{c^{\prime}}=\delta_{c}\setminus\{x\}
.

The derivation labelling the link in the bottom-right corner of the diagram is the same, independently of the sequence of coalescence steps.

Finally, we have the following special additional cases, in which the dualizer is not the same, but the proof nets are.

Appendix 0.B
To Witness or Not To Witness?

The choice of witnesses of the nominal quantifier rules
\nabla_{\mathsf{pop}}
and
\nabla_{\mathsf{load}}
should, in principle, be irrelevant for the proof, as the role of the nominal quantifiers is only to enforce freshness conditions.
So one may expect to be willing to identify derivations differing for the choice of the witness of nominal quantifier rules, as in the case of the
\alpha
-equivalence of bound variables.
That is, we may want to identify the two following derivations, which differ only for the choice of the witness of the nominal quantifiers.

{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 24.51718pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\kern 9.36938pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 40.04514pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$$}}}\kern 40.04514pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ax}\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to80.09027pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower Due to the similarity of the derivations above with the ones in
Equation

4
, and in view of the fact that the syntax of
\mathsf{PiL}
does not include function symbols, therefore witnesses are always variable, we can argue that also the choice of the witness of existential quantifier is negligible
5
5

More precisely, given an axiomatic linking for a sequent, it is possible to compute (if it exists) a witness map such in polynomial time using the unification algorithm for first-order terms.

,
as it does not change the topology of the proof net associated to the derivation.
Formally, we define the two following additional equivalence relations over derivations.

Definition 10

Let
\mathcal{D}_{1}
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}
be two derivations in
\mathsf{PiL}
.
We say that
\mathcal{D}_{1}
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}
are
equivalent modulo fresh name
if it is possible to transform
\mathcal{D}_{1}
into
\mathcal{D}_{2}
by changing the active term of the nominal quantifier rules and propagating the changes upwards in the derivation.
We say that
\mathcal{D}_{1}
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}
are
equivalent modulo witness assignment
if it is possible to transform
\mathcal{D}_{1}
into
\mathcal{D}_{2}
by changing the active term of the existential and nominal quantifier rules and propagating the changes upwards in the derivation.

We can prove that we can extend our local and strong canonicity results with the equivalence relations defined above by modifying the definition of our proof nets, i.e., both conflict nets and slice nets, by considering new definitions of
nominal
and
unification
proof nets, the latter in the spirit of Hughes’ unification nets
[
18
]
for multiplicative linear logic, the unification nets for purely additive linear logic from
[
13
]
, and combinatorial proofs for first-order classical logic
[
15
]
.

Definition 11

The
initial witness map

\mu^{\Lambda}
of a linking
\Lambda
is defined by letting
\mu_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}
be defined as follows:

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{\langle x\oc y\rangle,(z\wn t)\}
, then
\mu_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}=[x/z,y/t]
;

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{x,y\}
is a nominal link with
x
bound by
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
, then
\mu_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}=[x]y
;

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{\circ\}
, then
\mu_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}=\delta_{\varnothing}
.

We write
\delta^{\Lambda}\geq\mu^{\Lambda}
if for every link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
in
\Lambda
, we have
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}\geq\mu_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}
, and we may refer to proof nets as either conflict or slice nets.

A
nominal proof net
is a pair
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle

with
\mu_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}\geq\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}
for every link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
in
\Lambda
and such that the domain of each dualizer
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}
is a variable bound by an existential quantifier in the sequent
\Gamma
,
such that

\langle\tau(\Lambda),\mu^{\Lambda}\rangle
is a proof net.
A
unification proof net
is a coco-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
such that

\langle\tau(\Lambda),\mu^{\Lambda}\rangle
is a proof net.

Note however that for unification nets we weaken the coherence condition for coalescence, asking that the dualizers only are unifiable, and for nominal nets we restrict the condition of coherence for variables bound by the existential quantifiers only.

We conjecture that for equivalence modulo fresh name assignment, we should consider the following additional equivalence:

as well as the transformation on a derivation obtained by changing the witness of a nominal quantifier rule and propagating the change upwards in the derivation, as in the following example.
Similarly, for equivalence modulo witness assignment, we should consider the transformation on a derivation obtained by changing the witness of an existential quantifier rule and propagating the change upwards in the derivation.
